analysis.one_liner: Bans nearly all tobacco advertising, event sponsorship, and branded packaging to keep cigarettes away from young people.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to two House committees on July 16, 1996, sent to subcommittees ten days later, and left there until the 104th Congress ended, with 8 cosponsors and no recorded opponent.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it unlawful to advertise tobacco products at all — no magazine or billboard ads, no free samples or coupons, no brand-name sponsorship of sports or concerts, no paying for cigarettes to appear in movies or on toys and race cars. It would also have required plain packaging: no logos, pictures, or human figures, just black text on a white background. The bill's own findings state that tobacco kills about 450,000 Americans a year and that roughly 3,000 children try their first cigarette each day. It died in House subcommittees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face a tobacco market stripped of the $6 billion-a-year marketing machine the bill says hooks most smokers before age 18; families and taxpayers, who bear the roughly $65 billion in annual health care and productivity costs the bill cites; and state and local governments, which the bill explicitly allows to keep or tighten their own tobacco ad restrictions.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for anyone to advertise a tobacco product — ending magazine, newspaper, billboard, and point-of-sale tobacco advertising.

Bans free samples, coupons, and discounted tobacco; brand-name sponsorship of athletic, music, and artistic events; paid product placement in movies, TV, and video games; and tobacco logos on toys, vehicles, boats, and stadiums.
Requires plain packaging — no brand logos, pictures, or human figures, and only black print on a white background — removing the visual appeal the bill says drives youth smoking.
Backs the rules with enforcement: federal courts can issue injunctions against violators, and noncompliant products are treated as misbranded drugs under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
Explicitly preserves the right of state and local governments to regulate tobacco advertising locations and sales, so cities could still restrict billboards and transit ads.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would lose their advertising, promotion, sponsorship, and branded-merchandise channels — the bill says they spend over $6 billion a year on them. Advertising agencies, billboard and media companies, and the sports, music, and entertainment organizations paid to carry tobacco branding would lose that revenue, though existing sponsorship contracts got a phase-out of up to three years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco companies, ad agencies, and media

drawbacks.text: A near-total ban on advertising a product that remains legal for adults would almost certainly have drawn a First Amendment challenge under the commercial-speech doctrine, which courts have used to strike down broad ad bans, so the bill's core could have been narrowed or voided in court.

Adult smokers would lose all branding and product information, since packages could carry nothing but black text on white and no advertising of any kind would be allowed; the bill targets marketing, not the product itself.

Sports leagues, arts organizations, and media outlets that relied on tobacco sponsorship and ad dollars would take a real financial hit — the bill itself acknowledges this by letting contracts signed before enactment run up to three more years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the trade is strongly favorable: the bill's own findings put tobacco at 450,000 deaths and $65 billion in annual costs, with most smokers hooked before 18, and the costs fall almost entirely on tobacco companies and the businesses paid to carry their marketing, not on consumers. The honest caveats are the constitutional risk to a total ad ban and the lost ad and sponsorship revenue for media and event organizers, which are real but far smaller than the public health stakes.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, passed down to subcommittees, and simply sat there until the Congress ended — no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Representative James Hansen, a Utah Republican, introduced the bill on July 16, 1996, framing tobacco as an addiction that kills about 450,000 Americans a year and hooks most smokers before age 18.
It drew 8 cosponsors — 7 Democrats and 1 Republican — a small, bipartisan group for a sweeping advertising ban.

The Speaker referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee, and on July 26, 1996 it was sent down to the Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials and Health and Environment subcommittees.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, no markup, no committee or floor vote are recorded before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died with it.

Tobacco marketing continued untouched; the bill's findings noted the industry was already spending over $6 billion a year on promotion and that three decades of voluntary agreements had failed to curb it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and the advertising, media, and event-sponsorship businesses that profit from their marketing kept their channels intact, while the children the bill was written to protect gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and the ad industry

for.name: Rep. James V. Hansen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 16, 1996 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 8 House cosponsors (7 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to two subcommittees on July 26, 1996, and never brought it back for a committee vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: Held a concurrent referral of the bill and took no recorded action on it.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Actively opposed tobacco advertising restrictions and federal tobacco regulation during this period; no action by the industry on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and 7 of its 8 cosponsors were Democrats, but since no vote was ever taken, the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would have shut down every marketing channel — all advertising, free samples, coupons, sponsorships, product placement, branded merchandise, and logo packaging — that the bill says the industry uses to spend over $6 billion a year reaching new customers, most of them underage. Its interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the children it markets to.
Creating and placing tobacco ads in print, billboards, matchbooks, and point-of-sale displays would become unlawful, eliminating a large, high-spending client category.
Newspapers, magazines, and billboard operators would lose tobacco ad revenue outright, with billboards given a two-year phase-out.

Brand-name sponsorship of athletic, music, and artistic events would be banned, and tobacco branding could no longer appear on race cars, boats, stadiums, or toys — existing contracts got up to a three-year wind-down.
